summary: James Miller is a sinology and religious studies scholar who earned an M.A. from Cambridge (1997) and a Ph.D. from Boston University (2000). He served as Professor of Chinese Studies and Religious Studies at Queen's University Belfast (attested 2014).

James Morison was an Indologist who studied at Oxford, under Arthur Anthony Macdonell, and under Georg Bühler at the University of Vienna, earning his Ph.D. (~1889–1893). In 1914, he served as Librarian at Oxford's Indian Institute.

James Murdoch was a Japanologist and historian who studied at the University of Aberdeen (~1875–1879) and under Theodor Benfey (~1877–1878). He held posts at Kanazawa University (~1893–1898), the University of Tokyo (~1898–1900), and Kagoshima University (~1901–1908).

James Prinsep was an Indologist and historian who served at the Benares Mint (1820–1830) and the India Government Mint in Kolkata (1819, 1830–1838). He led The Asiatic Society (1832–1838) and founded the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal.

James Rennell was a scholar in Indology and history who served with the Bengal Engineers (1764) and surveyed Bengal for the East India Company (1764–1777). He founded the Royal Geographical Society in 1830.

James Robert Ballantyne was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the East India Company College, Edinburgh, and Glasgow (Ph.D. 1845). He served as Principal of Benares Sanskrit College (~1845–1861) and Professor at King's College London (1861–1864).

James Robson, a Buddhist studies, sinology, and religious studies scholar, earned his B.A. from UCSB and Ph.D. from Stanford (2002). After posts at Williams College and Michigan, he joined Harvard (~2008), becoming Harvard-Yenching Institute director in 2024.

James Roland Ware was a scholar in sinology, Buddhist studies, and Indology. He studied at the University of Pennsylvania and under Franklin Edgerton and Sylvain Lévi, later holding posts at Lehigh, University of Washington, and Harvard University (1932–1934).

James Smith Reid was a historian who studied at the University of Cambridge (~1865–1869). He held collegiate posts at Cambridge at Christ's College (1869–1880), Pembroke College (1873–1885), and Gonville and Caius College (1878–1926).

James Stark was a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as a Puisne Justice of the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka in 1840 and as President of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka in 1845.
James Stewart King was a scholar of Iranian and Central Asian studies and history. He was educated at Trinity College Dublin and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst (~1867–1868).

James Sutherland Cotton was an Indologist and historian who studied at Trinity College, Oxford (1867–1870). He served as Fellow and Lecturer at Queen's College, Benares, and held a post at Queens' College between 1871 and 1874.

James Taft Hatfield was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Northwestern and earned a Ph.D. from Johns Hopkins (~1887–1890). He taught at Rust College (1884–1885) and served as a professor at Northwestern University (1890–1934).

James Talboys Wheeler was a historian and Indologist. He served as Professor of Moral and Mental Philosophy at Presidency College, Chennai (~1858–1862), and became Assistant Secretary to the Government of India (~1862).
James Thomas Molesworth was an Indologist and linguist. He served as a linguist with the Bombay Native Infantry in 1814 and also held a linguist post with the Commissariat Department.

James Tod was an Indologist and historian who studied at the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, and under Gyanchandra. He served with the East India Company (~1799–1823) and was Librarian of the Royal Asiatic Society (~1823–1835).
James W. Benson is an Indologist and linguist. He held faculty and academic posts attested in 1999 and 2001 at Harvard University, the University of Oxford, and Wolfson College, Oxford.

James W. Heisig, a philosopher and religious studies scholar, earned degrees from Divine Word College, Loyola, Notre Dame, and Cambridge (Ph.D. ~1970–1973). He was a long-term Permanent Research Fellow at Nanzan University between 1976 and 2001.
James Ward was a philosopher who studied at Fitzwilliam College and Trinity College, Cambridge (~1869–1874). He held an academic post at the University of Cambridge from around 1897 until 1925.
James Whitehill is a scholar of Buddhist studies, religious studies, and philosophy who founded the Columbia Zen Center. He served as Professor of Religion at Stephens College (attested 2000).
